items.title: Bliki: Generated Glossary
items.author: Martin Fowler
items.content:
When we use LLMs in a specialized domain, such as the operations of any reasonably-large organization, there is a lot of specialized vocabulary. Such words and specialized meanings will be foreign to an LLM because they aren't in its training set, making it harder for the LLM to be effective when doing tasks in that domain. One technique to aid this is to use an LLM to generate a glossary of the terminology in that domain, and make this glossary available for any LLMs doing work in those circumstances.

The sources for the LLM can be any material within the organization concerned such as documents, emails, and chat logs. In some cases getting transcripts of audio or video may be helpful, although most organizations generate enough text to do the job.

The glossary-generating LLM should look for single words, and phrases of several words that regularly hang out together to form a meaningful term. The generator should be asked to identify terms that are new to it, but also known terms that are being used in unfamiliar ways. The latter can often cause the most confusion.

Once we have a list of specialized vocabulary we can ask the agent to produce a glossary, with definitions for each term. Some terms may be used in different ways, in which case the LLM should provide alternative definitions, with a note as to what context the differences appear in. The LLM can be asked to follow the output format of a dictionary, with a focus on precision and conciseness.

Once we have a draft glossary, then human experts in that domain should review it, and amend it for cases where the LLM has got the wrong ends of sticks.

We then put the glossary somewhere where any other LLM can use it. It should be in a form that's easy for the LLM to consult, and minimize the tokens the LLM should consume in order to find meaning. We should set up a schedule to review and refresh the glossary at regular intervals, by agents and humans. We should keep it in version control, so we can see how it changes over time.

Large organizations often have subtly different definitions in different places, essentially following the Domain Driven Design notion of Bounded Context. Source code can be a particularly interesting bounded context, allowing folks to understand how terminology is used within a code base. Sometimes a single glossary can span several of bounded contexts, but at other times it's better to have separate glossaries for each one, allowing LLMs to consult whichever glossaries that are relevant to what they are doing. I'd urge everyone to resist any temptation to create a single, standard, glossary - I've yet to see that work. Often the value of a glossary isn't to nail down a single definition of a term, but instead to highlight its different usage in different contexts.

When there are different bounded contexts it can be interesting to compare different glossaries, or to get LLMs to compare glossaries and describe differences in usage. Comparing a source-code derived glossary to a human text can be particularly instructive.

If the glossary is large, it can be worthwhile to only include the terms and links to definitions as part of the initial context. The model can then use the links for only the full definitions it needs while working.

A glossary can be used in several ways within Agentic Engineering. Glossaries can inform generation of code, so that names within the generated software fit the particular vocabulary of the enterprise. Sensors in a harness can check for this usage, both in the internals of the software and in the user-interface.

When generating code or documents, we may introduce new bounded contexts. For example, internal names that may be used within an organization should not be exposed in a customer-facing UI, because such internal terms are likely to be only confuse a customer. In this case a customer has a different bounded context to the part of the enterprise serving them.

It's often useful for glossaries to include terms that should not be used, in which case it includes advice on what other term to use instead. Terms that are deprecated can be handled in this way, with glossary entries that indicate what period of time a term should be in effect.

In my conversations with people working with agents in large organizations, a common theme is the difficulty of specialized language. This encourages the activities of domain modeling, building ontologies, and constructing explicit context layers in enterprise data. Getting LLMs to generate a glossary is a simple, but useful, part of this work.

Eric Nagler and Unmesh Joshi related their experiences doing this activity and thus inspired this post. Amy Pellegrini, Annie Luxton, Arun Srinivasan, Chris Ford, Daniel Terhorst-North, Dave Farley, Eric Nagler, James Shore, Jason Yip, Jimmy Nilsson, Matteo Vaccari, Michaël Le Barbier, Pete Hodgson, Pramod Sadalage, Ravi Vats, Unmesh Joshi, and Valentyn Logvynskyi commented on drafts.

items.title: Tests as data: ensuring AI-generated code does what we want
items.author: Martin Fowler
items.content: Automated testing in the age of AI coding assistants is problematic: when AI agents write both production and test code, developers risk losing the assurance that automated tests protect against functional errors. makes three claims: (1) when AI writes the code, developers become its customers; (2) therefore customer tests, not developer tests, become the primary contract between humans and AI; (3) moving that contract into test data rather than test code makes it easier to protect it from unexpected modifications by coding agents. All of this optimizes for human-readable tests that establish a contract between humans and AI. While in the past DSL parsers and custom test runners were expensive to write and maintain, now AI makes them cheap.

items.title: Fragments: November 10
items.author: Martin Fowler
items.content:
It’s that time of the year when the November Thoughtworks Technology Radar appears. Again my colleagues have taken a sweep of the technologies that our teams have used in the field, and pulled together a summary of what’s popped up in the last six months. It’s been a busy half-year, one that again has been dominated by AI, and that’s reflected in the many AI blips on the radar.

One team of passionate people experimenting with agents can make almost anything work. They share a context, a credit card and a mental model. They review each other’s work because they sit together, and they know what to check and how much latitude to give the coding agent.

Two hundred people, though, cannot work that way. The moment agentic AI becomes an operating model rather than a pilot, a second layer of problems appears: How is context shared between teams? What’s the token bill? How do we deal with increased review demands? What’s the agent allowed to reach, read and change? And who’s now responsible for the harness everyone depends on?

Experience so far suggests that the questions that enterprises face are about: shared context, token cost, cognitive load, security, and platform building. While these issues are distinct, they are not separate, so strategies to answer them must take all of them into account. I also echo Chris in reminding us that however impressive these tools are, we must remember that while we have to rethink systems and workflows to utilize these technologies, they should be built to serve humans - and we should all benefit from its bounty.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

I watch a lot of sports, and particularly this fall, watched a lot of baseball. My Milwaukee Brewers — excuse me, my World Champion Milwaukee Brewers — demanded my full attention, which also meant I saw a lot of campaign ads, and by far the most common topic, at least here in Wisconsin, was data centers. Moreover, it was never entirely clear which way it cut politically: both parties were anti-data center, accusing their opponent of being the opposite.

He points out that this opposition is recent, and tied to a shift in focus from the internet and streaming movies to AI:

you know, the technology that in the best case scenario is going to take everyone’s jobs, and in the worst case scenario end the human race.

There’s going to be a lot said about how Democratic officials will be at the heart of blocking data center building, but as his point above about campaign ads illustrates, the opposition to data centers is (at least at the moment) a bi-partisan opposition.

He follows up with “ten takes” from these consequences. The big beneficiaries of this opposition to building data centers will be those who own the data centers that have already been built. The opposition will reduce supply of tokens, meaning that token costs will go up, thus increasing the profits for those who already have their token generators plugged in and humming.

There’s also benefits to those who aren’t constrained by the need to build more big data centers. Other countries aren’t affected by a change in US policy, China is the most talked-about case here, but it’s not the only country that may benefit from a drop in US data center building. Apple may also benefit, if it means more AI work is pushed to edge devices that are their territory, in addition to having not sunk so many dollars into AI-specific investments.

To his analysis, I’ll add that this may also have a somewhat counter-intuitive effect on regulation, and corporate attitudes to it. The common expectation is that businesses are opposed to government regulation, since that interferes with their free pursuit of profit. That’s true to an extent, but it’s quite common to see established businesses lobby (quietly) in favor of regulation that acts as a barrier to new competitors. So I wouldn’t be at all surprised to see companies that have already built data centers to be pushing for regulations that impede or prevent new ones from being built.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

I hear a lot of suspicion that AI tokens are unsustainably priced and that frontier labs are heavily subsidising costs with their VC money. They want to get us hooked now, so they can pull the rug out from under us whenever they want to make a bunch of money. Is that true? My sense is that it’s mostly not. But can I back that up with some data?

His conclusion is that it doesn’t seem that token costs are significantly subsidized on per-token API basis, but they are with subscription plans. (He caveats his analysis, saying it doesn’t take into account recouping the costs of training the models.)

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

While we don’t know if we’ll ever be able to download skills directly into our brains (“I know kung fu” - or for those in my particular demographic: Joe 90), this does raise the possibility of downloading capabilities into models by manipulating their weights.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

My days of teaching AI to do stuff are numbered.

Getting it to teach me stuff is more fun.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Houck et al (that “al” includes some folks who I’ve learned to pay a lot of attention to), look at how we can assess the quality of context supplied to agents.

An agent may draw from source code, specifications, issue trackers, chat histories, architectural documents, tool output, and user instructions, then act on that combination with limited human supervision. Information that was written for different audiences, at different times, and for different purposes is brought together into a temporary operating environment for a particular task. Whether each source is individually useful does not reveal whether the resulting context is fit for the work the agent is being asked to do.

  • Clarity: Can the agent interpret the request as intended?
  • Actionability: Can the agent proceed, and know when it is done?
  • Fidelity: Can the agent trust that this context is true?
  • Efficiency: Can the agent focus on what matters?
  • Security: Should the agent have this context at all?

They also list a set of half-a-dozen “context smells”: common cases where these break down (and a nod to Kent’s original metaphor)

I’m not sure about the name, (how exactly should I pronounce “CAFE(S)”?) and the article exhibits rather more LLM Voice that I prefer. But on the whole I think this is a good framing for thinking about an important part of feeding our silicon servants/overlords.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

What was missing in my setup 6 months ago was the verification process I now use.

70% of my daily token spend goes into verifying patches, and only ~20-30% into creating them.

That resonated with conversations I’ve had with folks using agents in enterprise settings. They are using far more tokens to check the working of models (through guardrails and evals) than they are to generate a response to a request. A single request to a model from a customer may trigger a dozen turns to other models to probe its input and verify its output.

items.title: Long-horizon agents and durable execution
items.author: Martin Fowler
items.content: Long-horizon agents can automate complex tasks that take days or weeks to complete and involve multiple exchanges with people and external systems. Many things can go wrong during this time, including process crashes, network failures, and unanticipated real-world behavior. explains durable execution: an emerging pattern that helps agents recover from these failures and move towards their goal. In this programming model, the runtime keeps a record of the result of each step that interacts with the outside world so that, when a failure occurs, the program runs again, completed steps are skipped, and the program's state is rebuilt from the record.

items.title: The Data Product Platform Navigator
items.author: Martin Fowler
items.content: Many organizations adopting data mesh and data products face a common challenge. They may be tasked with building a self-service platform for data products and data mesh from scratch, or they may have an existing platform that suffers from low adoption, preventing their data mesh from scaling. This article provides a platform navigator, based on the CNCF's Platform Engineering Maturity Model, to help you reason about your current situation and determine the next steps for your platform.

items.title: Bliki: LLM Voice
items.author: Martin Fowler
items.content:
Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion

There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present.

I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales ,” or “a round-up of news”. But I've heard these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit, don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.)

Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction. Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that be ok, but only as far as an outline. Authors should fill the prose themselves.

Say Your Writing is even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering to an LLM will undermine any progress.

In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence. I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then?

Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes to this site). He finds working with an LLM is essential to his writing to overcome the bane of Parkinson's disease. I'll gladly deal with LLM-Voice in order to continue imbibing my old friend's wisdom.

A more awkward case is that of translation. Many of my colleagues aren't comfortable in English, it is their second or fourth language. Some have found LLM translation an important part to their communication with those of us who know rather less Marathi. But I also would prefer rather a genuine human's clunky prose to the smooth but soulless LLM.

There are situations where it would be reasonable for even a native Englishman to let LLMs write the prose. Such as if I'm writing a form letter to an official, or preparing a report I suspect no-one will ever read . Maybe most documentation in the future will only be read by LLMs, and they won't have my uncanny valley worries. But if I want to communicate with humans, my humanity has to shine (or at least ooze) out of my prose.

Alessio Ferri, Caer Sanders, Ian Cartwright, Jie Jessie Xia, Joshua Kerievsky, Michael Feathers, Michael Nygard, Scott Davies, and Wei Zhang commented on drafts of this post.

I did not use AI or LLMs in any way while writing this post.

items.title: Why are good developers so wary of agentic development?
items.author: Rachel Laycock
items.content:
Good developers’ caution about agentic development comes from knowing that built isn’t the same as working in production.

I’ve been surprised by how many excellent developers have been hesitant to go all in on coding agents. These are people who usually try new ways of working before anyone else and in many cases invent new tools and practices that support building the application well. So why have we had so much reluctance?

The easy (lazy?) answer is that they love writing code, or they’re worried about their jobs. I’m sure that’s true for some people, some of the time. And I know it is true for some of the developers I talk to but I always felt there was something else, another fear hiding behind those obvious ones. When we put together the Technology Radar every six months I try to block out a chunk of time for us to do an open space. In September, a discussion we had on agentic development, which pushed it to its limits, finally helped me see clearly what that fear is.

Thoughtworkers care deeply about building the right thing and building it right. It’s pretty much our default way of working and thinking and it’s where many of the practices and technologies we invented and championed came from. We want software that is useful and helpful, can be changed next year, and doesn’t fall over in production. Our developers adopted, championed or invented some of the first versions of continuous integration, pairing, automated testing, continuous delivery, microservices and many others early because they helped us build the software right.

Early coding agents made it very easy to produce code, including code we wouldn’t have wanted anywhere near production, written by people who have not learned about the chasm between building something and making it run in production safely. The tools have improved enormously, but experienced developers still have questions. Are we confident this is the right behaviour? Does it work as expected? Are these the right boundaries? Will we be able to evolve it? Does it abide by the principles and practices we learned the hard way to give us confidence it will meet the needs of the customer and stay up in production? What happens when something fails? Will another team be able to live with it? And so on.

Underneath all of those sits a bigger question. How much can we trust a system when nobody has experience of building it this way? Let me state that another way. Nearly every system we have in production now was built the old way, by hand, by people we could trust (hopefully). Everything we build now is the new way and we have not lived with that yet.

After more than 25 years in technology, I’ve come to value the judgment people develop through experience. I regularly put similar questions to models and to senior technologists at Thoughtworks. For the difficult questions, I still get more useful answers from the humans or maybe more insightful with very specific experience that helps me better understand the point. They challenge the premise, recognise a pattern from something that went wrong ten years ago, or spot the organisational problem hiding inside the technical one. I can now access an extraordinary amount of information. I still need people who can help me think through what matters, I still need wisdom and insight. That type judgment is exactly what hesitant experienced developers are trying to protect.

And I want to be clear: they are not hesitant to use a coding assistant, they are hesitant to go all in and let the agents do all the execution. They are hesitant to take their hand off the wheel because they don’t have full confidence the agents have the right guardrails in place to run off on their own.

Recently, Giles Alexander, our Regional CTO for Europe, brought senior engineers, infrastructure consultants and product people together for a week of working in exactly this way. No code written by anyone. Everything built by agents. The point wasn’t to prove that an airline application could be built in a week. (Funnily enough they got 80% done and we all know what that means… you can’t make stuff up!) The purpose of the experiment was to learn what happens to the team’s work when agents do all of the coding. You can read some of what they learned here.

What struck me in our conversations was how much time they spent at the whiteboard. Working out the domain. Drawing boundaries. Deciding what should happen next and making plans the agents could act on. Meanwhile, the agents kept producing code beyond the team’s working day.

The humans were also designing the feedback around that work: tests, contracts, architecture checks and a delivery pipeline. They were working out how to give agents enough freedom to make progress while keeping confidence in the result. Most of the work at the keyboard was directing agents to put this learning into the harness, so the building and testing agents got it right on the next run and they could have more confidence in what they built. Interestingly in the end the product person committed more feature code than anyone else on the team.

When I asked them to estimate they said they spend about ⅔ of their time at the whiteboard and ⅓ on the harness, which could give us some clue as to how developers will work in the future, but before you get ahead of yourself redesigning your team, that’s not the end of the story…

The application ran. The build was red.

The application ran, but the build was frequently red. It worked on their machine - again you couldn’t make this up if you tried! A constant red build gives me the ick. A red build should mean something: stop, investigate, fix it. If it’s red so often that people stop paying attention, how do we spot the next real failure? And if we can’t trust the checks, a green build stops being reassuring too. That’s exactly the uncertainty continuous integration was supposed to remove, and we’ve been advocating it for over 25 years.

We’re still working through how to address it. Remember this was an experiment to push the very edge of agentic development. Were too many agents working in parallel and stepping on each other’s changes? Was the system not yet modular enough for agents to work on separate parts? Or were changes simply arriving faster than the checks could finish? Or was it a combination of all of these and more? Either way we definitely need to rethink how we will solve the last mile challenges. I can see continuous delivery/DevOps as a movement having a resurgence and a rethink in the agentic era in the same way the rest of the development life cycle is being upended. And it isn’t just our experiment. DORA’s 2025 research found AI adoption is now linked to higher delivery throughput, but to lower delivery stability. Exactly what continuous delivery and DevOps were trying to solve for!

All of these challenges prompted some good arguments internally. What role should test-driven development play when you aren’t reading every line and the agent created the tests alongside the code? Where would acceptance tests, contract tests and checks at system boundaries give us more confidence without being too brittle? How much design should we do before setting an agent loose, given how quickly we can revise an approach? Is there an appropriate point we will know we have gone too far? One of the biggest puzzles in all this is the size of the batch. I have heard many teams are moving from Stories to Epics. Great for speed of development but can your CI pipeline handle that size unit of work at speed and in parallel?

The experiment team didn’t settle all of this in a week or even two (they ran it twice with different teams). I wouldn’t trust anyone who claimed they had. But this is exactly the kind of work I want experienced developers involved in: experimenting, questioning and helping us discover which practices hold up and where we need some new ones.

After coming away from this conversation with some of the senior developers involved I kept thinking about learning to ski. Kids will often head straight down the hill without fear, kind of like a new builder who has never put software into production and has never fixed an on-call issue at 3am (something I will never forget, right up there with every production issue I personally caused and the resultant learnings from those, which are burned in my brain forever). When I first tried to ski as an adult, I was thinking about what I might break. I wanted to ski, it looked so fun and freeing, but I was old enough to see the consequences and I didn’t fancy hobbling around London with a broken limb or worse. My biggest issue was I hadn’t yet learned how to turn or stop effectively and without that I was a runaway train on a ski slope.

When I shared a draft of this post with Martin, who also learned to ski late, he pointed out where the comparison breaks down (like all analogies I like to push them to the edge, pun intended). On a ski slope you’ve watched countless people reach the bottom with no broken bones. The instructors have taught thousands of people before you on the same slope. They know which skills matter and how to teach them. Agentic development right now is more like a backcountry trip across unknown territory. We don’t yet know which skills will matter most. Not many people, if any, have finished the trip safely and the feedback on how to navigate it is slow or non-existent. As Martin put it, we won’t know whether a heavily agent-built system works until it has run in production for a while, survived a few rounds of change, and not sent all our planes to Aberystwyth. Built is not the same as working in production. Or as Charity Majors puts it, “staging is just a glorified laptop. Only prod is prod”. Which is why when someone says “it works on my machine” it’s usually intended as a joke. Or at least I always laugh.

That solidified a nagging discomfort I have had with leaders, technical or non-technical, claiming devs aren’t curious, or are laggards slow to adopt, and putting that down to easy-to-point-at fears like missing writing code (I do too) and fearing for our jobs (who isn’t right now?). Our best developers aren’t nervous beginners on a nursery slope that everyone else has already mastered. They’re looking at unmarked terrain and asking sensible questions about the route. Telling them to be less cautious misses the point. They need to be on the team that maps it.

Of course, experience can also make us too attached to familiar practices. Some of what we learned on the groomed slopes won’t hold out there, and we need to be willing to test our assumptions.

A challenge for both sides

So there’s a challenge here for both leaders and developers. Leaders need to listen carefully enough to tell useful concerns from reluctance to change, and to create real room for experimentation. That means time, permission to get things wrong, and not judging success by how much code the agents produced. Developers need to bring their experience into those experiments and be prepared to find that some of their assumptions no longer hold.

Some familiar practices will become more important. Others will need a different shape. Nobody is going to hand us a map first.

If you care deeply about building the right thing and building it right, your judgment is exactly what this new way of working needs. Bring the caution. Then let’s set off into the snow.

items.title: Fragments: October 28
items.author: Martin Fowler
items.content:
The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

Many of my colleagues are living in a world where LLM capabilities are stunning, but it’s easy to forget that’s not what most people experience. One thing I do is use free-tier LLM chatbots, and I’m still finding that while most of the time they are useful, their unreliability undermines much of that usefulness. Yes, you can argue that I’m not using frontier tools or a forceful enough harness, but that’s true of most regular folks too. To understand their perception, it’s handy to experience it.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

That observation particularly resonates with me today, as I’ve just spent the weekend at Foocamp, an open space event run by O’Reilly. It was full of those who are experiencing that vertigo of LLM capabilities, so it felt very much like being in a bubble of those on the bleeding edge. While it’s worth remembering that that’s not a typical view of what’s happening, it’s good to see what those explorers are experiencing. (As I talk about this, I’m applying the Chatham House rule, if anyone wants attribution, let me know.)

A couple of folks talked about doing immersion courses to help teach developers how to do agentic engineering. The idea is to get people out of their usual work environment, and spend one or two weeks with experienced coaches, learning how to use these tools well. Such things remind me very much of the Extreme Programming immersion classes I was involved with at the turn of the century. As with that, the experience of building something is important to understand such a new style of work.

Unsurprisingly the coaches observed that the biggest impact wasn’t technical, but emotional. New tools are just new tools, but tools change basic assumptions of what it means to be a software developer, which for many people challenges their identity. One coach said how his main job was to take such people out for a walk to a coffee shop, so they could process what’s happening. (This reminds me of a participant of the Extreme Programming immersion who was so horrified by the use of a non-locking version-control system (CVS) that he walked out of the class on the first day.)

I’m wary of talking about themes to an event where I attend less than one-tenth of the sessions, but a topic I kept coming across was how large enterprises were embracing this technology - or rather not. One participant used a lovely metaphor: corporations have acquired a Swiss-army knife, but are only using the toothpick. I see plenty of decent reasons for this: it’s one thing for a startup or individual to use a hot technology, but there’s a big difference between a website going down and your factories grinding to a halt. Big organizations involve workflows involving lots of people that have built up over many years - they don’t change easily. Security concerns abound, the lethal trifecta still lurks.

In particular good use of AI in enterprises relies on good data, and many such organizations don’t have their data in a decent shape. The path to getting agent-ready data isn’t trivial and it’s hard to see how we can get the knife and saw out until enterprises are much further down that path. One thing that struck me is that there was little conversation about this at Foocamp - a sign of its visibility among the people there.

I very much enjoyed Foocamp, but events like this are always a mix of excitement and dread. I knew very few of the people there, so it was a great opportunity to get out of my own social bubble. But I also find it nearly impossible to walk up to people I don’t know (or know slightly) and impose my company on them. The great thing about unconferences is that the nature of the sessions make it plausible for someone like me to engage in conversation during them, and begin some tentative links. Also I thank the many folks there who were friendly to me as I casually walked around trying to hide how much I was panicking.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

On Saturday, Apollo’s chief economist Torsten Slok published No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector. It’s short and it’s blunt: outside of 7 major tech companies, there is no data yet to support a productivity gain that justifies all the money pouring into tech.

My position is that he’s half right: are valuations too high? Absolutely. We’re in a bubble, and it’s absolutely going to pop. But does that mean investing in AI is a waste of money? Absolutely not, and using this early data to try and decide that question would be like trying to decide in 1997 whether the Internet was going to pay off. The data just isn’t there yet, because these things take time.

I’m not as sure as he is that we can peg today to 1997 rather than 1999, but I agree that this boom bears a lot of resemblance to the dotcom boom (although I think this one is bigger). While many dotcom companies crashed (I always think of pets.com and webvan) he’s right to point out that anyone who invested in Amazon in 1997 did very well. Where might those good investments be this time?

if you can build something that proves you got the answer, AI can get the answer much faster than you can, and there are real productivity gains to be had doing that generally.

As we think about this, remember that investment isn’t just buying shares, but also where we choose to invest that precious resource of our time and energy.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

For me, agentic coding is enjoyable because it lets me take on larger parts of a problem than I would have been able to master manually. Infrastructure updates are no longer a blocker. And I don’t need to spend time learning about a build system I never cared about.

My personal goal is to get better at working with higher-level abstractions, and accept that writing code is likely to be a dying skill. My bet on the future is that our problem solving skills, logical mindset, and understanding of systems will be at least as rewarding.

In the end, we only need to challenge our identity if we mistake programming for writing code. AI finally allows us to separate the two. And that’s where all those years of experience transfer the best: knowing not only what to build but how to build it well.

For me (and I’m not alone), the biggest issue isn’t what GenAI can and can’t do, it’s the ethical and economic discomforts. This technology is being peddled by terrible people who are rich and whose goal is to get richer. It’s bought and deployed by terrible people who want to slash their payrolls by throwing thought workers onto the street. It facilitates the oncoming climate catastrophe and devalues human creative effort.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Annie Vella observes that the change we’re seeing in software development follows a way of thinking about automation that goes back to the 1960’s as the distinction between direct and supervisory control.

The main difference between direct and supervisory control is that in the latter, there’s a computer that closes the loop instead of a human operator. Before AI, writing software was much more like direct control - we closed the loop ourselves. We interpreted requirements, made changes to the code, received feedback and acted on it, over and over. Now, coding agents can increasingly close that loop themselves - writing code, running tests and fixing their own mistakes - while we move towards supervisory control: telling the agent what we want, keeping an eye on how it’s going and taking over when we need to.

She outlines various ideas that this intellectual thread developed. The five-level model developed by Endsley and Kiris seems apposite:

In AI-assisted software development
The early days of AI coding assistants’ autocomplete
AI coding agents where you must approve the actions they take
Auto-mode, with the ability to veto the coding agent’s actions
Full auto-mode, such as might be used in a dark software factory

Vella cautions that this comes with an important caveat:

There is one notable difference between the automation described by this prior research and the type of automation that AI agents give us. Both sets of levels assume that the computer’s account of what it did is accurate and honest. As we all know by now, what an AI agent says it did and what it actually did may not be the same thing. Still, it’s automation, and it still requires supervision - arguably more, since we can’t simply take its word for it.

Vella’s conclusion from all this is that: “our next step must be to start redesigning the job and the system, in tandem”. I agree with this, and the Foocampers’ immersion courses I mentioned earlier are part of that exercise. The tricky thing is that we don’t yet know what this new job design looks like, but I think Vella is on the right path when she says:

What if we stopped thinking of the SDLC as a process we follow, and instead started thinking of it as a control system we build and supervise?

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

A while ago I mentioned how much I enjoyed Eric Evans’s keynote at DDD Europe. Now the video is available so those who weren’t in Antwerp can watch it.

He opens by looking at our future, saying that rather than fruitlessly trying to predict it, we should instead explore it with “curiosity, fun, and wonder”. He’s been doing this, digging deeper into the theory and fundamentals that underpin AI.

He goes into detail on his side project: the Domain Language Surveyor. The idea is to be able to examine different repositories, and analyze the vocabulary used inside those repositories to see if they are related bounded contexts. To do this he built a pipeline of tools, illustrating how a useful system blends both computational and inferential components. He then used this pipeline to analyze the vocabulary of some open-source healthcare codebases, to see how their bounded contexts related.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

A topic that regularly comes up when I talk to companies outside the Foocamp world, is the cost of tokens, and the concern about how that cost is going to increase in the future. We’ve been worrying about that at Thoughtworks, and my colleague Andy Nolan describes our token sourcing strategy, which we forecast will reduce our token costs in 2028 from $16-40M down to $6.8-1M.

The strategy rents frontier models for the work that needs frontier-level reasoning. It runs open-weight models, on capacity we choose, for the work that carries our IP or runs at a volume where owning the capacity costs less.

The strategy involves looking at each LLM workload, and classifying it on two axes: domain differentiation and security & sovereignty. We then place each workload on a nine cell grid.

The nine cells run from the cheapest capable API, swapped as prices change, to a fine-tuned open model on our own infrastructure, with full control and full upkeep. For a given workload, the highest score on a given axis determines the right position in the grid. There is no single right place for all workloads. Each organization ends up with its own distribution and mix of workloads across the grid.

items.title: Fragments: October 21
items.author: Martin Fowler
items.content:
Gergely Orosz is frustrated at those that entered his explicitly “No AI” essay competition and used AI. He goes on to say:

When I start to suspect some part is AI about someone I don’t know: how can I tell how much of it is? And how much time and effort do I want to invest to figure out?

I fear most people do not realize this last part: that when it takes time and effort from others to figure out what % is AI, and what % is YOU, then I will simply assume it’s probably 100% AI and 0% you

So when producing anything that is meant for other humans, if you use even a little AI, you risk the assumption that it is all AI and pointless to pay attention to

In general, I agree with him, and react much the same. Once I hear LLM Voice, I flip the bozo bit and check out of the post.

But as I do this I have caveats. How accurate is my neural net at AI-detection, are humans taking on AI-ish elements in their normal communication? And more seriously there are some valid uses for AI. Jim Highsmith’s story of his second brain helping him deal with Parkinson’s is one. Another is folks who don’t know English well, using AI to translate. Am I being unfair when I flip the AI voice bit when I read/listen to them?

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

I was sad to hear that the Grace Hopper Celebration is canceled this year. It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code. Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut.

In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation:

Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts.

One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at

having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed.

She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data.

Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier.

The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug.

The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control

A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments.

With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses.

The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution.

Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies.

This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans.

A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent

Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on.

And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent

In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to

While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.
